extracted.intended_audience: literary critics, poets, and students of poetry/literature
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic guidance and evaluative criteria for reading, judging, and composing Romantic-era poetry (especially Wordsworth): distinctions of poetic faculties (fancy vs imagination), stylistic virtues and faults, and how to weigh individual poems within a collected work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid judging whole work by a few inferior poems
rubrics_metrics.description: “it was assuredly hard and unjust to fix the attention on a few separate and insulated poems ... instead of passing them over in silence, as so much blank paper”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let a few weak or isolated pieces determine your assessment of an entire volume; treat such pieces, if not immoral or indecent, as 'light or inferior coins in a rouleau of gold' rather than as alloy corrupting the whole. Criticism should weigh the whole work and not magnify small defects into a verdict on the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject affected simplicity and trivial associations
rubrics_metrics.description: Be wary of “a downright simpleness, under the affectation of simplicity, prosaic words in feeble metre, silly thoughts in childish phrases, and a preference of mean, degrading, or, at best, trivial associations and characters.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authentic simplicity differs from an affected, counterfeited simplicity. Avoid prosaic diction, weak metre, childish phrasing, and trivial or degrading associations presented as poetic virtue; these traits produce a false, inferior poetry that can nevertheless mislead imitators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody should be intelligent, not mere silliness
rubrics_metrics.description: “to conceal and convey wit and wisdom in the semblance of folly and dulness ... is doubtless a proof of genius ... but the attempt to ridicule a silly and childish poem, by writing another still sillier ... can only prove ... that the parodist is a still greater blockhead.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good parody masks intellect under apparent dullness or folly and can show satiric talent; bad parody merely copies silliness and thereby demonstrates poor judgement. Imitators should balance likeness with corrective difference to constitute a just imitation rather than caricature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish fancy from imagination; value imagination's unity
rubrics_metrics.description: “The fancy brings together images which have no connexion natural or moral ... The Imagination modifies images, and gives unity to variety.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or composing poetry, identify whether the work is driven by fancy (associative, accidental juxtapositions) or imagination (power that modifies images and creates unity). Imagination is preferred for producing unified, meaningful poetic effects; fancy can produce mere ornamental or incoherent assemblages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize types of imagination (epic vs dramatic) and their effects
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an “epic imagination, the perfection of which is in Milton; and the dramatic, of which Shakspeare is the absolute master.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics and poets should note the kind of imagination at work: epic imagination creates a comprehensive, unifying vision (Milton), while dramatic imagination stamps all nature with a single meaning within character and action (Shakespeare). Each type entails different virtues and techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive obscurity and forced diction
rubrics_metrics.description: The “novelty and struggling-crowd of images, acting in conjunction with the difficulties of the style, demands always a greater closeness of attention than poetry ... has a right to claim” and “justified the complaint of obscurity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style should not be so knotty, contorted, or overloaded with images that it demands an unreasonable closeness of attention. Forced diction and contortion that produce obscurity are faults; clarity and controlled imagination are preferable unless obscurity is knowingly and fruitfully employed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance deep feeling and profound thought
rubrics_metrics.description: The excellence consists in “the union of deep feeling with profound thought; the fine balance of truth in observing, with the imaginative faculty in modifying the objects observed.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great poetry combines sincere emotion with reflective thought, and balances truthful observation with imaginative transformation. Evaluate works by whether they achieve this union rather than privileging feeling or thought alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create atmosphere and an ideal world around incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Possess “the original gift of spreading the tone, the atmosphere and with it the depth and height of the ideal world around forms, incidents, and situations.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poet's ability to diffuse tone and atmosphere—to surround events and characters with an imaginative ideal world—is a mark of strength. Look for pervasive tonal/atmospheric effects that enlarge ordinary incidents into the poetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider an artist's developmental stage; early faults may be temporary
rubrics_metrics.description: “The poetic Psyche ... undergoes as many changes ... It is remarkable how soon genius clears and purifies itself from the faults and errors of its earliest products.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging early works, allow for developmental faults (harshness, obscurity, illogical phrases) that may be the ferment by which later maturity is achieved. Criticism should sometimes be tempered by the poet's stage of growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for subjective variability in reception
rubrics_metrics.description: The same work provoked wide disagreement: “the composition which one cited as execrable, another quoted as his favorite.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about treating popular or critical consensus as definitive; reception can vary widely between readers and over time. Individual poems may divide opinion—this variability should influence, not dictate, critical judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form influences diction and reader associations
rubrics_metrics.description: “the Spenserian stanza ... would, doubtless, have authorized ... a more frequent descent to the phrases of ordinary life, than could ... have been hazarded in the heroic couplet.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be sensitive to how form (stanza, meter) carries stylistic associations that authorize certain diction or approaches. Choose forms with awareness of their historical/associative effects; critics should note when form shapes language and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use precise vocabulary; disambiguate synonyms to avoid equivocation
rubrics_metrics.description: When “two distinct meanings are confused under one and the same word ... we must either invent or borrow a word” to appropriate meanings and prevent erroneous consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarity depends on distinguishing senses of similar words and, when necessary, coining or adopting distinct terms. Writers should avoid equivocation that leads to false inferences; critics should attend to semantic slippage that affects argument or poetic meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'bulls'—incongruous juxtapositions without connective sense
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'bull' consists in “bringing together two incompatible thoughts, with the sensation, but without the sense, of their connexion,” produced when attention isolates each conception and ignores intermediate notions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevent absurd or unintentionally comic juxtapositions by ensuring genuine associative or logical links between images and concepts. The critic should note when juxtaposition is arbitrary (fancy) versus when it is synthesized into imaginative unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admire on principle to imitate without losing originality
rubrics_metrics.description: “To admire on principle, is the only way to imitate without loss of originality.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists should analyze and adopt underlying principles (not surface mannerisms) of admired work so imitation leads to principled influence rather than mere copying. Critics can guide artists by elucidating these principles.
